name: COPPA: Children Under 13
title: COPPA: Children Under 13
answer: COPPA requires companies to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children under 13, but schools can consent on parents' behalf only when the data serves a school authorized educational purpose and no commercial purpose. This matters because the company, not the school, carries final legal responsibility, yet students are the ones exposed when a company mishandles their data. The rule was updated in 2025 with full compliance required by April 22, 2026, adding separate consent for third party sharing and limits on how long children's data may be kept.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: COPPA is the federal rule that governs how websites and apps may collect personal information from children under 13, requiring verifiable parental consent first. Schools get a shortcut: the school itself can give that consent for parents, but only when the information is used for a school authorized educational purpose and nothing commercial. The FTC recommends that this decision be made by the school or district rather than by individual teachers, and that parents be told which services have been approved. The idea solves a practical problem, because asking every parent to consent to every tool would be unworkable, while letting companies collect children's data freely would leave students unprotected. It also settles who is accountable, placing final responsibility for compliance on the company rather than the school.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the district or school leadership reviews and approves the services students will use, then notifies parents about which ones have been approved, rather than leaving each teacher to make that call alone. The consent the school gives is valid only while the tool is used for a school authorized educational purpose and not for advertising or other commercial purposes. Because many general chat tools require users to be at least 13, and some require parental permission for anyone under 18, age shapes how AI is used by grade band. UNESCO's guidance recommends 13 as the minimum age for independent conversations with generative AI, so most AI use in the early grades belongs with the teacher rather than the child. This is why the Volume lists age rules for every named product.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text cites the Federal Trade Commission (2020) for the school consent shortcut and its limits, and the Federal Trade Commission (2023) for an action against Edmodo, which the FTC said had about 600,000 users under 13 in 2020 alone, for collecting children's information without proper consent, using it for advertising, and pushing its COPPA duties onto schools and teachers. The agency stated plainly that the company, not the school, bears final responsibility for complying. The rule was updated in 2025, with full compliance required by April 22, 2026, per the Federal Register (2025), requiring separate parental consent before sharing a child's information with third parties such as advertisers and limiting data retention to what is reasonably needed. The FTC considered adding specific rules for education technology but set them aside, pointing to possible changes in FERPA, and a separate bill often called COPPA 2.0 would extend protections to teens up to 16 but had not become law as of this writing.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The school consent shortcut has a hard limit: it applies only when information is used for a school authorized educational purpose and for no other commercial purpose. Even with that shortcut, the company bears final responsibility for complying, so a school still has every reason to check because its students are the ones exposed when a company gets it wrong. The decision to approve a service should rest with the school or district rather than individual teachers, and parents should be told which services the school has approved. Age rules remain a limit on practice, since many general chat tools require users to be at least 13 and some require parental permission under 18, and UNESCO's guidance recommends 13 as the minimum age for independent conversations with generative AI. The FTC set aside specific education technology rules, and COPPA 2.0 had not become law as of this writing, so these boundaries rest on the current rule and the judgment of the adults responsible.
